slides: Before you practice, here's a quick summary of the topic. How to read a definition, the types of questions, and the shortcuts.

slides.say: A new operation is just a definition. Read it, and then follow the whole rule. Whatever goes in takes the place of the letter, in every spot, and in brackets. Diamond of x is x squared minus five x. So diamond of negative two is negative two, squared, minus five times negative two. That's four plus ten, which is fourteen.

Read which input goes in which slot. a heart b is three times, in brackets, a plus b, so four heart two is three times six, eighteen. And the order can matter, so don't assume that two star five is five star two.
Inside a longer exercise, turn each operation into a number first. And nested operations go from the inside out. The inner result becomes the outer input, so don't stop halfway.
When the operation works on an expression, match the whole input first. F of four t is t plus three. For F of twenty, four t is twenty, so t is five, and the answer is five plus three, eight.

When an input and its result are given but the rule is missing, put that input into each candidate rule. When only a property is given, like doing the diamond twice brings back x, apply each candidate twice. And when the input is unknown, write the definition, and it's an ordinary equation.

When the rule has conditions, check which rule to use at every step, because the input changes. When we go backwards, from the result to the input, try every rule, and keep an answer only if it fits the rule it came from.
When the rule uses itself, go down to the start value, then climb back up. When the operation is on both sides of an equation, treat it as one unknown and isolate it.

When the question asks what is not always true, one allowed example where a choice fails is enough. When it asks what must be true, a failing example rules a choice out, and when all the other choices are out, the one that's left is the answer. So plug in an easy allowed value, check the choices right away, and use another value only if more than one choice is left. To see why a rule always works, use algebra, and when the question is about the order of the inputs, swap the letters. And skip a question only if its calculation would really take long.

Some rules undo themselves, as long as every step stays where the operation is defined. Six over x does, for positive x. Ten minus x comes back too, but not for every positive x, because ten minus twenty is negative. And an inverse operation undoes the steps in reverse order.

A value minus its value at the opposite number? The terms with even powers of x and the plain number cancel, and the terms with odd powers of x double. And look for the shortcut formulas inside a definition. [pause] That's it. Now go practice, and I'll see you in the next video.
